top_evidence.document_title: Systematic review of direct access physiotherapy for musculoskeletal conditions in primary care: consequences for general practitioner workload, resource use, and organisation of care
top_evidence.text: The initial search was conducted from 15 July 2024 to 15 October 2024. To ensure currency of evidence, an updated search was performed from 1 January 2024 to 4 November 2025, capturing any late-indexed records from the original search period and newly published studies. Searches covered databases (MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, CINAHL, PEDro, Web of Science, Scopus, Cairn.info, Érudit, ClinicalTrials. gov) and discovery platforms (ScienceDirect, Google Scholar). Grey literature was identified through structured searches of Google Scholar (using predefined search equations consistent with the main database strategy), clinical trial registries (ClinicalTrials.gov and WHO ICTRP), and French-language platforms (Cairn.info, Érudit), which index professional and institutional literature not systematically covered by international biomedical databases (see Additional file 2).

top_evidence.document_title: Systematic review of direct access physiotherapy for musculoskeletal conditions in primary care: consequences for general practitioner workload, resource use, and organisation of care
top_evidence.text: The combined searches identified 7,264 records (7,239 from databases and 25 from trial registries). After removal of duplicates, 5,003 unique records were screened. The initial search (15 July-15 October 2024) contributed 6,811 records; the updated search (1 January 2024-4 November 2025) yielded 453 additional records but no further eligible primary studies, likely reflecting evidence base stabilization and publication lag. After screening and eligibility assessment, 21 studies were included. The PRISMA 2020 flow diagram of study selection is presented in Fig. 1. The final sample comprised 7 randomised controlled trials (RCTs) and 14 observational studies. Two economic evaluations published separately were linked to their respective parent RCTs for all quality and certainty assessments to avoid double counting.

top_evidence.document_title: Systematic review of direct access physiotherapy for musculoskeletal conditions in primary care: consequences for general practitioner workload, resource use, and organisation of care
top_evidence.text: Background Musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs) are frequent and disabling conditions in primary care and contribute substantially to general practitioners' (GPs) workload. Direct access (DA) to physiotherapy, allowing patients to consult physiotherapists without prior medical referral, has been proposed to streamline care, reduce delays, and optimise resource use. This systematic review synthesized the effects of DA on GPs' practice and the organisation of primary care for adults with MSDs. Methods Following PRISMA 2020, we systematically searched 12 databases/platforms (MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, CINAHL, PEDro, Web of Science, Scopus, Cairn.info, Érudit, ClinicalTrials.gov) and discovery platforms (ScienceDirect, Google Scholar), plus grey literature, from 15 July 2024 to 4 November 2025 (initial search 15 July-15 October 2024; updated search 1 January 2024-4 November 2025). Eligible studies assessed the consequences of DA to physiotherapy for MSDs in primary care versus GP-referred pathways (referral-based usual care). Two reviewers independently screened, extracted data, as well as appraised quality using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (observational studies), ROB 2.0 (RCTs), and graded certainty using GRADE at the study level. Outcomes included GP workload, imaging and medication prescriptions, clinical results, costs, and safety. Results We included 21 studies (7 RCTs, 14 observational) totaling 90 401 patients (15 017 DA; 75 384 GP-referred). Across 15 studies, DA was associated with 10-30% fewer GP consultations. 14 studies reported reduced imaging and medication use under DA; effects on prescriptions were context-dependent. 14 studies showed non-inferior clinical outcomes, with small early advantages in some RCTs. 13 studies assessed costs, indicating neutral to reduced perepisode costs; two RCT-linked economic analyses were comparable or favorable to DA. No serious adverse events attributable to DA were reported (5 studies). GRADE certainty was moderate in 2, low in 12, and very low in 5 studies, *Correspondence: Matthieu Fischer matthieu.fischer.75@gmail.com Full list of author information is available at the end of the article BMC © The Author(s) 2026. Conclusions In adults with MSDs, DA to physiotherapy appears to lessen GP workload and resource use with clinical outcomes similar to GP-referred pathways and no consistent signal of increased harms. Given methodological limitations, further robust comparative studies are warranted to inform large-scale implementation and policy in primary care. top_evidence.document_title: Systematic review of direct access physiotherapy for musculoskeletal conditions in primary care: consequences for general practitioner workload, resource use, and organisation of care
top_evidence.text: Two reviewers (MaF and EB) independently screened titles/abstracts and then full texts using Rayyan for webbased screening and duplicate detection [26]; disagreements were resolved by consensus. For the updated search (1 January 2024-4 November 2025), a pragmatic single-reviewer approach (MaF) was adopted at title/ abstract level given the short timeframe. To assess reliability, a random 20% sample ( n = 13/65) was independently screened by a second reviewer (EB), yielding excellent inter-rater agreement (Cohen's κ = 0.91). All potentially eligible records were subsequently assessed at full text by both reviewers independently.

top_evidence.document_title: Systematic review of direct access physiotherapy for musculoskeletal conditions in primary care: consequences for general practitioner workload, resource use, and organisation of care
top_evidence.text: Data were extracted using a standardised form adapted from the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions (version 6.3) [27], with pre-specified units/ scales (e.g., VAS 0-10 or 0-100, ODI 0-100, MSK-HQ 0-56, EQ-5D index) recorded as reported. Extracted items included authors, year, country, design, sample, intervention/comparator, outcomes, measurement tools, sources of funding, declared conflicts of interest, and key quantitative results. Participants were counted once per unique study or cohort to avoid double counting when the same cohort was reported across linked publications (e.g., primary study and linked economic evaluation) or contributed data to multiple outcomes. For transparency, all study-level quantitative results used to populate the SoF are reproduced verbatim in Additional Tables S1-S7, with units and time windows preserved. Two reviewers (MaF and EB) independently extracted data and reconciled discrepancies by consensus.

top_evidence.text: This systematic review followed Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 [24]. In accordance with PRISMA, we prepared outcome-specific Summary of Findings tables (SoF) that collate study-level results per outcome and are provided as Additional Tables S1-S7. The protocol was prospectively registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF; ID 897ub; 15 August 2024, available at h t t p s : / / o s f . i o/ 8 9 7 u b / ) [25]. The completed PRISMA 2020 checklist is available in Additional file 1.
